extracted.intended_audience: educated readers seeking moral and practical guidance (householders, parents, people managing servants or families)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical guidance for personal conduct—particularly managing anger, chastisement, courage, and judging exceptional acts—drawn from Montaigne's essays. Emphasises alignment of life with principles, timing and measure in punishment, and how belief and premeditation affect behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live according to your doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosopher endeavours to make his life correspond with his doctrine (i.e., practice what one preaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives examples of philosophers who behaved with outward constancy (e.g. maintained indifference to danger). He notes difficulty: it is one thing to imagine stoic attitudes, another to join the effects, and still harder to make them habitual. The ideal is not mere profession but consistent conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imagination from habitual constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagining or attempting stoic indifference is insufficient; forming habitual constancy in conduct is rare and almost incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a philosopher who continued and finished discourse though his interlocutor left; facing physical injuries without wincing. Montaigne warns that joining effects to imagination is difficult and making them habitual is extraordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge exceptional acts in cultural and intentional context
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts such as self-immolation or ritual suicide must be assessed with regard to cultural custom, premeditation, and professed purpose (religion, honour, public ceremony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts diverse customs (Indian widows, Cybele priests, gymnosophists) to show that what appears monstrous in one culture may be honoured in another; premeditation and communal framing alter moral perception. He advises caution before condemning such acts absent context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate divine prescience with necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing or foreseeing an event (even by God) does not cause it; knowledge is not causation, and foreknowledge does not negate free will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explains the theological point that God’s prescience lists causes including voluntary actions; belief in predestination may nevertheless be used pragmatically (e.g., commanders encouraging soldiers), but logic and moral responsibility remain distinct from fatalistic rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the true signs of anger
rubrics_metrics.description: True anger is indicated by physical manifestations (face, colour, voice, foaming, trembling); absence of these signs suggests the person is not truly angry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Plutarch’s anecdote: when confronted about seeming contradiction, a philosopher calmly points out there is no redness, foam, tremor, or dreadful voice — these are the ‘true signs’ of anger. Use these observable markers to judge whether someone is genuinely moved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never punish while angry; delay chastisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lay hands upon servants or children while your anger lasts; defer punishment until you are calm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion commands and speaks, not reason; faults seen through passion appear larger. Chastisement should be like medicine (physic), not revenge. Montaigne gives examples (Plato, Archytas) where those who would punish excuse themselves because they are angry, and advises waiting until pulse and emotion subside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure chastisement is measured, purposeful, and reaches the offender
rubrics_metrics.description: Chastisement must be inflicted with discretion and weight, aimed at the person truly at fault; avoid lavishing anger indiscriminately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated or rash scolding runs into custom and becomes despised; make sure the reproach reaches the offender (don’t scold before he arrives or continue after he’s gone). Too-frequent punishment loses effect; be deliberate and ensure the target is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty, performative rage (save ranting for the offender)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not huff and vapour without an enemy; reserve rhodomontades for discharging upon the offending party rather than rehearsing the fight to no effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne condemns loud rehearsal of anger (like a bull butting a tree) which only vents and never chastises the real party. Such display is ineffective and often self-defeating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of vices is more dangerous than their openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices are less pernicious when open; simulacra of good nature that hide vice are most dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Seneca: “All vices are less dangerous when open to be seen, and then most pernicious when they lurk under a dissembled good nature.” Montaigne prefers uncovering passions rather than brooding inwardly, because inward brooding damages oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer authenticity of agent when evaluating advice, but judge content too
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess both the speaker and the sermon: a man who does what he preaches persuades more than one who only writes or speaks without having practised it; yet a wicked man may preach truth and a virtuous man may err in opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Brutus vs Cicero — the lived example strengthens persuasion. Montaigne warns against dismissing truths merely because of the minister’s vices, but affirms the rhetorical power of lived conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunger, thirst, and bodily needs impair just chastisement
rubrics_metrics.description: One who intends to punish should not be under hunger or thirst when administering chastisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that chastisement inflicted while hungry or thirsty (or generally under bodily perturbation) is less just and more likely to be motivated by passion than by measured correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and prepare to resist passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation, expectation, and fortification help repel violent passions when they arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne says he can contain himself for great occasions by fortifying and preparing in advance; but when passion seizes unexpectedly, it carries him away. He advises internal provision, not only outward composure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger can be excused or useful in certain roles if tempered
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger is always an imperfection but more excusable in soldiers; sometimes anger serves as an instrument for virtue and valour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Aristotle and military examples, Montaigne allows that in some trades (soldiers) anger may be functional; the point is moderation and context-sensitive judgement rather than blanket condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared or concurrent anger escalates conflict; allow each person their own way
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger provokes further anger; disputes are escalated by mutual passion, so granting individuals their way can prevent storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes storms are begot by concurrence of angers; pragmatic household rule: when you see someone moved, let them alone for a time — reciprocal restraint keeps peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigning anger can be a deliberate governing tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes one may put on a seeming anger strategically to govern a household without real emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne admits to sometimes feigning anger to better govern his house; this is presented as a practical (if ethically ambiguous) device distinct from genuinely being carried away by passion.
